In dynamic and partially observable environments, effective communication is crucial for reducing uncertainty and enabling coordination. While research in multi-agent communication (MA-Comm) spans diverse methods and paradigms, its central challenges can often be understood through the guiding lens of the Five Ws of communication: who talks to whom, when to speak, what to convey, and why communication is beneficial. These questions provide an intuitive thread across different approaches, even when not used as explicit section divisions. Progress in this field has been rapid. Within the Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) framework, early work emphasized static, hand-designed protocols, while later approaches introduced trainable, end-to-end communication models optimized with deep learning. This shift sparked interest in emergent language, where agents develop symbolic or structured messaging strategies through interaction. More recently, large language models (LLMs) have opened new possibilities, enabling natural language as a medium for reasoning, planning, and collaboration in more open-ended environments. Despite this momentum, there is still no dedicated survey that brings together these different lines of work. Most existing reviews focus narrowly on MARL, without fully addressing how communication is evolving from simple message passing to symbolic reasoning and language use. This paper aims to fill that gap. We provide a structured survey of MA-Comm, spanning traditional MARL approaches and emergent language studies. In dynamic and partially observable environments, effective communication is crucial for reducing uncertainty and enabling coordination. While research in multi-agent communication (MA-Comm) spans diverse methods and paradigms, its central challenges can often be understood through the guiding lens of the Five Ws of communication: who talks to whom, when to speak, what to convey, and why communication is beneficial. These questions provide an intuitive thread across different approaches, even when not used as explicit section divisions. Progress in this field has been rapid. Within the Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) framework, early work emphasized static, hand-designed protocols, while later approaches introduced trainable, end-to-end communication models optimized with deep learning. This shift sparked interest in emergent language, where agents develop symbolic or structured messaging strategies through interaction. More recently, large language models (LLMs) have opened new possibilities, enabling natural language as a medium for reasoning, planning, and collaboration in more open-ended environments. Despite this momentum, there is still no dedicated survey that brings together these different lines of work. Most existing reviews focus narrowly on MARL, without fully addressing how communication is evolving from simple message passing to symbolic reasoning and language use. This paper aims to fill that gap. We provide a structured survey of MA-Comm, spanning traditional MARL approaches and emergent language studies. In light of growing interest in agentic and embodied AI, we also examine how LLMs are reshaping communication in both MARL contexts and broader multi-agent ecosystems. By using the Five Ws as a conceptual lens, our goal is to clarify the landscape, highlight key trends, and provide a foundation for future research at the intersection of communication, coordination, and learning in multi-agent systems.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.36227/techrxiv.175760290.08279849/v1\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2025, 9, 11]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7648642\", \"title\": [\"HealthGuard-MARL: Emergent Sleeper-Cell Fraud in a Multi-Agent Healthcare Insurance Market A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework for Real-Time Healthcare Fraud Detection\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Healthcare fraud costs the United States an estimated $300 billion annually [1]. Current detection systems are retrospective and static, failing against adaptive, patient adversaries. We present HealthGuard-MARL, a multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) framework in which a saboteur hospital agent discovers a sleeper-cell fraud strategy: behave honestly to accumulate trust, strike with inflated claims at peak trust, absorb the penalty, and repeat, entirely through reward maximisation, with no scripted fraud instructions. We replicate the Kerr &amp; Cohen (2006, 2009) Value Imbalance attack in a healthcare trust-audit simulation and make four original contributions: (1) a 30-seed significance test demonstrating the strategy is statistically robust (paired t(29) = 9.36, p &lt; 10-6 , Cohen's d = 1.71, 100% directional consistency); (2) a three-metric behavioural distinctness test showing the learned policy is qualitatively different from a maximum-intensity hand-coded threshold rule (all p &lt; 0.0001, Bonferroni-corrected); (3) a learning insurer that decisively defeats the sleeper (19/20 vs. 1/20 runs, non-overlapping CIs); and (4) a monitoring-cost phase transition that governs who wins the arms race. Declaration of generative AI use. The authors used a generative AI assistant (Anthropic Claude) during this project for software development support, including drafting and refactoring simulation and analysis code, generating figure-plotting scripts, and copy-editing the manuscript. All research questions, experimental designs, pre-registered hypotheses, result interpretations and conclusions are the authors' own. The authors reviewed and verified all generated code and all reported output, and take full responsibility for the content of this paper.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7648642\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.54499/2022.14163.bd\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.54499/2022.14163.bd\"}, {\"DOI\": \"10.21236/ada401850\", \"title\": [\"Information Dynamics and Emergent Behavior of Heterogeneous-Agent Systems\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.21236/ada401850\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2001, 12, 1]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "0abd40b359ef5878bf09703feb53abed31ee2d77a124272a8058133165891252", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "emergent_preferences", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.36227/techrxiv.175760290.08279849/v1", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.7648642", "doi:10.54499/2022.14163.bd", "doi:10.21236/ada401850"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.36227/techrxiv.175760290.08279849/v1", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7648642", "https://doi.org/10.54499/2022.14163.bd", "https://doi.org/10.21236/ada401850"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
